title: Porto on foot, from the Clérigos tower to the river: what is free and what needs a ticket
subtitle: A downhill walk from the station to the cathedral, the Ribeira and the bridge, with the doors that cost money marked.
excerpt: A half-day walk through the old centre of Porto, from São Bento station and the Clérigos tower to the cathedral, the Ribeira and the Dom Luís I bridge: what you see for nothing, which doors need a ticket, and what the partner sells.
secondary_keywords: Dom Luís I bridge on foot

is the Clérigos tower worth climbing
can you walk across the Dom Luís I bridge

meta_title: Porto on foot: what is free and what needs a ticket
meta_description: A downhill walk in Porto: São Bento, the Clérigos tower, the cathedral, the Ribeira and the bridge. What is free, and which doors need a ticket.

featured_image.alt: The houses of old Porto climbing to the cathedral and the bishop's palace, with the upper deck of the Dom Luís I bridge in the foreground

content_html:
[place attraction="porto-cathedral" city="porto"]

Nicolau Nasoni was a painter from Tuscany who arrived in Porto in 1725 to decorate the cathedral, and never left. Over the next forty years he gave the granite city its Baroque face: palaces, fountains, church fronts. For the Brotherhood of the Clérigos, a charity that looked after poor priests, he built a church on a steep and awkward plot, and behind it, finished in 1763, a bell tower about 75 metres high. For a long time it was the tallest building in Portugal, and ships coming up the Douro steered by it.

Nasoni took no fee for the work. He joined the brotherhood, died poor in 1773, and was buried in the church he had designed. His tower is still the best way to understand Porto before you walk it: a city on two hills, with a river far below. The practical question is which of its doors are worth paying for, because most of what makes the walk is free.

How the walk is laid out

The old centre is small and steep. If you start at the top and finish at the river, almost everything is downhill, and three hours are enough without going inside anywhere. Add an hour for each ticketed stop.

The order that works: São Bento station, up to the Clérigos tower, back down and across to the cathedral, down the stairs to the Ribeira, then over the bridge to Vila Nova de Gaia. Wear shoes with a grip. The paving is polished granite and the stairs are uneven.

What is free

  • São Bento station. The entrance hall is lined with about twenty thousand painted tiles by Jorge Colaço, set between 1905 and 1916: battles, a royal entry into Porto, and scenes of country life along the top. It is a working station, so you simply walk in.
  • The Clérigos church. The oval church in front of the tower is free. Only the tower and the museum rooms behind it need a ticket.
  • The cathedral square. The terrace beside the cathedral looks over the roofs to the river and costs nothing. The cathedral itself was begun in the twelfth century and looks like a fortress, which in part it was. In 1387 King João I married Philippa of Lancaster here.
  • The Ribeira. The riverside quarter of tall, narrow, tiled houses, part of the historic centre that UNESCO listed in 1996. The stairways that drop to it from the cathedral are the oldest streets in the city.
  • The Dom Luís I bridge. Opened in 1886 and designed by Théophile Seyrig, who had been a partner of Gustave Eiffel. It has two decks. The lower one carries cars and has pavements. The upper one carries the metro and pedestrians, with no barrier between the two, so keep to the side.
  • The view from Gaia. The quay on the far bank, lined with the names of the port houses, gives the classic picture of Porto. Higher up, the terrace by the round church of Serra do Pilar gives a wider one.

The hall of São Bento station. You walk in from the street, with or without a train to catch. Photo: John Samuel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What needs a ticket

The Clérigos tower

A narrow spiral of a little over two hundred steps, with no lift, and a balcony at the top that holds few people at a time. The ticket also covers the museum in the house of the brotherhood. In season there is a line at the door, and late afternoon is the worst hour. The view is the best in the city, because it includes the cathedral.

From the top of the Clérigos tower: the cathedral and the white bishop's palace on the hill opposite. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The cathedral cloister

The nave of the cathedral has usually been open without charge. The ticket is for the Gothic cloister, whose walls were covered in the eighteenth century with blue and white tile panels, and for the rooms around and above it. If you pay for one interior on this walk and do not mind missing the tower's view, this is the calmer choice.

The west front of the cathedral: two towers, a rose window and very little else. Photo: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The cloister, with its blue and white tile panels. This is the part behind the ticket. Photo: Daniel Villafruela, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Stock Exchange Palace and São Francisco

Near the river, the nineteenth-century Palácio da Bolsa is visited only on guided tours at fixed times, for its Arab Room. Next door, the church of São Francisco is Gothic outside and covered inside with gilded carved wood. Both sell their own tickets.

The port lodges

Port is made far up the Douro valley, and aged across the river from Porto, in Vila Nova de Gaia, where the barrels used to arrive by boat. Each lodge sells its own visit with a tasting, usually at a fixed time and in a set language. Book directly, and before lunch if you still plan to climb back up.

What the partner's listings include

  • A cathedral ticket with an audio walk includes entry to the cathedral's ticketed part and an audio route through the city in the partner's app. The commentary is for the streets: the listing says it does not cover the inside of the cathedral.
  • A Clérigos tower and museum ticket with an audio city walk works the same way: entry to the tower, and a walk that carries on to the river. No commentary inside the tower.
  • The audio walks, on the old city, on port wine, on tiles, are commentary only, on your own phone. Entry tickets for the places they pass are bought elsewhere. Bring earphones.

These are the Porto tickets and audio walks our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="porto" match="cathedral,clerigos,highlights,history" limit="5"]

Getting back up

The walk ends at the bottom of a hill. There are three ways back:

  • cross to Gaia on the lower deck, climb or take the cable car to the upper end of the bridge, and walk back over the upper deck, which lands you close to the cathedral;
  • take the funicular that runs from the foot of the bridge on the Porto side up to the old town wall;
  • walk up Rua das Flores, a long pedestrian street that climbs gently back to São Bento.

The cable car and the funicular are paid. The street is not, and it is the most pleasant of the three.

When to go

Start in the morning. The station hall and the cathedral terrace are quiet before ten, and the tower has no line early. The Ribeira faces south and is at its best in late afternoon, when the light is on the houses and the Gaia quay is in shade. Opening hours for the cathedral change with the season: see our page for Porto Cathedral.

From here

From the Gaia end of the Dom Luís I bridge the riverside promenade runs west past the lodges. Back in Porto, the tiled church fronts of Santo Ildefonso and Carmo are free to look at, and São Bento has trains up the Douro valley for a second day. See what else there is in Porto, or open the trip planner for Portugal.

Cover photo: Michael Gaylard, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: What is free to see in Porto?
faqs.a: The tiled hall of São Bento station, the Clérigos church, the cathedral square and its view, the Ribeira, both decks of the Dom Luís I bridge and the quay of Vila Nova de Gaia are all free.

faqs.q: Is Porto Cathedral free to enter?
faqs.a: The nave has usually been open without charge. The cloister with its tile panels and the rooms around it need a ticket. Check the current arrangement before you go.

faqs.q: Is the Clérigos tower worth climbing?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are comfortable on a narrow spiral of a little over two hundred steps with no lift. It gives the best view of the city, cathedral included. Go early to avoid the line.

faqs.q: Can you walk across the Dom Luís I bridge?
faqs.a: Yes, on both decks, for free. The lower deck has pavements beside the cars. The upper deck is shared with the metro, with no barrier, so keep to the side.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk the old town of Porto?
faqs.a: About three hours from São Bento station to the river and across the bridge, without going inside anywhere. Add about an hour for each ticketed stop.

title: City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia: which ticket to buy, and what you can see for free
subtitle: Three ticketed buildings, six ways to combine them, and a walk between them that costs nothing.
excerpt: The City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia sells entry to three separate buildings, alone or combined. How long each one takes, who each is for, which combination fits your day, and what you see without any ticket.
focus_keyword: City of Arts and Sciences which ticket
secondary_keywords: City of Arts and Sciences combined ticket
City of Arts and Sciences free
longtail_phrases: which ticket to buy for the City of Arts and Sciences
is the City of Arts and Sciences free to walk around
how long do you need at the Oceanogràfic
is the Hemisfèric worth it
can you do the Oceanogràfic and the science museum in one day
meta_title: City of Arts and Sciences Valencia: which ticket
meta_description: Oceanogràfic, science museum or Hemisfèric: how long each takes, which combined ticket fits your day, and what you can see in Valencia for free.

featured_image.alt: The Hemisfèric in Valencia, a glass and white concrete shell shaped like an eye, reflected in its pool at dusk

content_html:
[place attraction="city-of-arts-and-sciences" city="valencia"]

On 14 October 1957 the river Turia burst its banks twice in one day and flooded most of Valencia. At least 81 people died. The government in Madrid decided that the river would never run through the city again, and over the following years it was moved into a new channel to the south. That left a dry riverbed, several kilometres long, curving through the middle of town.

The first plan was to put a motorway in it. People in Valencia campaigned for years under a slogan that said the riverbed was theirs and they wanted it green, and they won: from the 1980s it became a long park. At its seaward end, from 1998 onwards, the region built the City of Arts and Sciences, designed mostly by Santiago Calatrava, who was born in Valencia. It looks like one place. For a visitor it is three paid attractions with separate doors, sold alone or in every combination, and a good deal of open space that is free.

What is there

The complex is a line of white buildings about two kilometres long, set in shallow pools. From west to east:

  • The opera house (Palau de les Arts), opened in 2005. You go in for a performance or a guided visit.
  • The Hemisfèric, opened in 1998: the building shaped like an eye. Inside is a single domed hall that shows large-format films and planetarium programmes.
  • The science museum, opened in 2000: the long ribbed building, with three floors of hands-on exhibits.
  • The Umbracle: a raised garden walk under white arches, along the south side.
  • The Àgora, the tall blue building, which now houses an art centre with a ticket of its own.
  • The Oceanogràfic, opened in 2003, at the far end: the aquarium, under shell-shaped roofs designed by Félix Candela.

The science museum along its pool. Walking here costs nothing, at any hour. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What you can see for free

All of the outside. You can walk the whole length of the complex, along the pools, under the ribs of the museum, across the bridges and through the Umbracle, at any hour, without a ticket. The buildings are the main sight, and they are best in the last hour of daylight and just after, when the pools are still and the lights come on.

The Turia park itself is free too. From the old town it is a flat walk or bicycle ride of about three kilometres along the riverbed, under the old bridges, to the opera house.

The arches of the Umbracle, the free garden walk on the south side. Photo: Sjaak Kempe, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The three tickets, one by one

The Oceanogràfic

The largest aquarium in Europe, laid out as separate pavilions around a lake, each for one sea or climate: the Mediterranean, the tropics, the Arctic with its belugas, the wetlands under a netted dome, two long underwater tunnels. Allow three to four hours. Much of the walking between pavilions is outdoors, so it is tiring in the midday heat of July and August. It is by far the most expensive of the three, and the one children remember.

The science museum

Its motto is that it is forbidden not to touch. The exhibits are built to be handled, which suits children from about seven and curious adults, and leaves toddlers with little to do. Allow two hours. It is indoors and cool, which makes it the choice for a wet day or a very hot afternoon. If you only want the architecture, the ground floor hall can be seen from the entrance.

Inside the science museum: open floors under the white ribs. Photo: Steven Lek, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Hemisfèric

A film of about three quarters of an hour on a huge curved screen. The ticket is for one session at a fixed time, and the programme changes through the day, so look at what is showing before you choose. Commentary in other languages comes through headphones. It is the cheapest ticket and the shortest visit, and it fits in the gap before or after one of the other two.

Which combination for which day

  • Two hours, no children. Walk the outside for free. Add the Hemisfèric if a film interests you.
  • Half a day with children. The Oceanogràfic alone. Go at opening time and do the outdoor pavilions first.
  • A full day. The Oceanogràfic in the morning and the science museum in the afternoon, when you want to be indoors. This is the combination most people are happiest with.
  • All three. Possible in one day only if you start at opening and book a late film. Check whether your combined ticket lets you use the parts on different days: if it does, split them.
  • A rainy day. The science museum and the Hemisfèric, which are next to each other.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Single tickets are sold for the science museum, for the Hemisfèric and for the Oceanogràfic. "Skip the line" here means you do not queue at the ticket desk. Everyone passes the same door.
  • Tickets for two pair the Oceanogràfic with the Hemisfèric, or with the science museum.
  • The ticket for three covers all the paid buildings named above except the opera house and the art centre.
  • None of these includes a guide. Before paying, read on the listing how the film session is chosen and for how long the parts stay valid.

These are the tickets our partner sells for the City of Arts and Sciences, with today's prices:

[partner city="valencia" match="ocean,hemisf,science" limit="6"]

Getting there and around

City buses run from the centre to both ends of the complex, and a taxi from the old town takes about ten minutes. On foot or by bicycle, follow the Turia park. The Oceanogràfic is at the eastern end, a quarter of an hour's walk from the opera house, so decide where you start before you get off the bus. There is little shade between the buildings: in summer carry water and a hat. Opening hours change with the season and are on our page for the City of Arts and Sciences.

From here

The beaches of Valencia are a short bus or taxi ride further east. Back up the riverbed, the old town holds the cathedral, the Silk Exchange, a Gothic trading hall on the UNESCO list, and the Central Market, which is free to walk through in the morning. Our pages for the Oceanogràfic and for Valencia have more, and the trip planner for Spain fits the city into a longer route.

Cover photo: Diliff, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5.

faqs.q: Is the City of Arts and Sciences free to walk around?
faqs.a: Yes. The outside of the whole complex, its pools, bridges and the Umbracle garden walk are open without a ticket. Only the insides of the Hemisfèric, the science museum and the Oceanogràfic are paid.

faqs.q: Which ticket should you buy for the City of Arts and Sciences?
faqs.a: With children and half a day, the Oceanogràfic alone. For a full day, the Oceanogràfic with the science museum. The Hemisfèric is a short film that fits before or after either.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the Oceanogràfic?
faqs.a: Three to four hours. The pavilions are spread around a lake and much of the walking between them is outdoors.

faqs.q: Is the Hemisfèric worth it?
faqs.a: It is one film of about three quarters of an hour on a very large curved screen, at a fixed time. It is worth it if a film in the programme interests you. The building itself is seen for free from outside.

faqs.q: Can you do the Oceanogràfic and the science museum in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. Do the Oceanogràfic in the morning and the museum, which is indoors, in the afternoon. Adding the Hemisfèric as well makes a very long day.

title: Genoa's old port: the aquarium, the Bigo lift and the Biosphere, and which tickets are worth it
subtitle: Three paid attractions on one quay, a house of Columbus up the hill, and a free old town between them.
excerpt: What the Aquarium of Genoa, the Bigo panoramic lift, the Biosphere and the Columbus House each give you, how long they take, which ones to skip on a short day, and what in the old town of Genoa is free.
longtail_phrases: is the Bigo lift in Genoa worth it
how long does the Aquarium of Genoa take
what is the glass ball in the port of Genoa
is the Columbus House in Genoa worth visiting
what to see in Genoa for free
meta_title: Genoa's old port: aquarium, Bigo, Biosphere tickets
meta_description: The Aquarium of Genoa, the Bigo lift, the Biosphere and the Columbus House: what each gives you, how long it takes, and what is free around them.

featured_image.alt: The white steel arms of the Bigo rising from the water of the old port of Genoa under a grey sky

content_html:
[place attraction="aquarium-of-genoa" city="genoa"]

For most of the twentieth century the people of Genoa could not reach their own harbour. The old port, where the city began, lay behind customs walls and warehouses, and in 1965 an elevated road was built along the whole waterfront, between the palaces and the sea. The medieval alleys stopped at a fence.

The change came in 1992. Five hundred years after the first voyage of Christopher Columbus, who was born here, Genoa held an international exhibition on the sea, and the job of preparing the port went to Renzo Piano, another Genoese. He opened the quays to the public, turned the cotton warehouses into halls, and added an aquarium and a strange white structure of masts. The road is still overhead, but you walk under it in a minute. What Piano left is a waterfront with several ticket desks, and it helps to know before you arrive which of them deserve your time.

What is on the quay

The aquarium

The long building on its own pier, and the reason most visitors come. It is one of the largest aquariums in Europe, with around seventy tanks: sharks, seals, penguins, jellyfish, a shallow pool where rays come to the surface. It has been extended twice, first with a ship moored alongside, then in 2013 with a pavilion for dolphins, also by Piano. The route runs one way and takes about two and a half hours.

The shallow pool of the rays, in one of the darker halls. Photo: Francesco Crippa, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Bigo

The white arms that lean out over the water are modelled on a ship's derrick, which in the port of Genoa was called a bigo. One of them carries a round glass cabin that rises about forty metres and turns slowly through a full circle. The ride lasts about ten minutes. From the top you see how the city is made: the port, the dense grey roofs of the old town, and the hills with their forts behind.

The Biosphere

The glass ball floating beside the aquarium was added by Piano in 2001. Inside is a small piece of tropical forest: tree ferns, a few birds, turtles, butterflies. It is twenty metres across, and a visit takes a quarter of an hour.

The glass ball of the Biosphere and, beside it, the long building of the aquarium. Photo: Bbruno, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which are worth it

  • The aquarium: yes, if you give it the time. It is expensive and deserves a half day. Entry is by time slot, and the middle of the day is the fullest, with school groups in spring. Book the first slot or a late one. If you have only an afternoon in Genoa and no children with you, spend it in the old town instead.
  • The Bigo: yes, as a first stop. It is cheap and short, and it works as a map of the city before you walk into it. If you would sooner not pay, the terrace of Castelletto, reached by a public lift from Piazza del Portello, gives the other classic view, from the hill down to the sea.
  • The Biosphere: only with small children. It is pleasant and very small. Adults see most of it through the glass from the quay.

The Columbus House

This one is not on the quay. It stands fifteen minutes' walk inland, at the foot of Porta Soprana, the twin-towered gate of 1155. Columbus lived on this spot as a boy, when his father was a wool weaver. The house you see is not the one he knew: that was wrecked when a French fleet bombarded Genoa in 1684, and what stands now was rebuilt afterwards on the same site.

Inside there are two small floors and a visit of ten to fifteen minutes. Go for the place and its story, not for what is on show. The gate, and the ruined cloister of Sant'Andrea beside the house, are seen for free from the street.

The house of Columbus: two small floors, rebuilt after the bombardment of 1684. Photo: Enric, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is free

  • The quays themselves, with the old cotton warehouses and the view back to the city.
  • Palazzo San Giorgio, the painted palace facing the port, begun in 1260. Tradition says that Marco Polo, taken prisoner by the Genoese, dictated his travels here.
  • The Cathedral of San Lorenzo, with its black and white striped front. In the right aisle stands a British naval shell that came through the roof in February 1941 and did not explode. The treasury below has a ticket.
  • The alleys, called caruggi: one of the largest medieval centres in Europe, still lived in, with shrines on the corners. They are safe by day. Keep to the busier ones after dark.
  • Via Garibaldi, the sixteenth-century street of palaces that UNESCO listed in 2006. Walking it and looking into the courtyards is free. Three of the palaces form a museum with one ticket.

The striped front of San Lorenzo. The cathedral is free to enter. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Aquarium tickets come as plain entry, and as entry with a lunch or with a street food tasting. On the last two, read where and when the food is served before you choose a time.
  • The Bigo, the Biosphere and the Columbus House are each sold as a separate fast track ticket. "Fast track" means the ticket is already in your hand. None of them takes long to enter in any case.
  • The partner also has audio walks through the old town. They are commentary only, and entry to anything on the way is bought separately.

These are the tickets our partner sells in Genoa, with today's prices:

[partner city="genoa" match="aquarium,bigo,biosphere,columbus" limit="6"]

A day in order

Take the Bigo first, for the view. Do the aquarium at your slot. Then walk under the elevated road to Palazzo San Giorgio, up Via San Lorenzo to the cathedral, on to Piazza De Ferrari and its fountain, and round the corner to Porta Soprana and the Columbus House. Finish on Via Garibaldi. The whole route is about two kilometres and mostly flat. Current hours are on our page for the Aquarium of Genoa.

From here

From the old port, boats leave in season for Camogli, San Fruttuoso and Portofino. The sea museum at the western end of the harbour sells its own tickets. Trains along the coast reach the Cinque Terre in about an hour and a half. See the pages for Genoa Cathedral, Palazzo San Giorgio and the rest of Genoa, or open the attractions map of Italy.

Cover photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Bigo lift in Genoa worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, as a short first stop. The glass cabin rises about forty metres and turns through a full circle in about ten minutes, which shows you the port, the old town and the hills at once.

faqs.q: How long does the Aquarium of Genoa take?
faqs.a: About two and a half hours on the one-way route. Entry is by time slot, and the first and last slots of the day are the quietest.

faqs.q: What is the glass ball in the port of Genoa?
faqs.a: It is the Biosphere, added by Renzo Piano in 2001. It holds a small tropical garden with ferns, birds and butterflies, and takes about a quarter of an hour to visit.

faqs.q: Is the Columbus House in Genoa worth visiting?
faqs.a: It is a visit of ten to fifteen minutes on two small floors. The house was rebuilt after the bombardment of 1684 on the site where Columbus lived as a boy, so go for the place and not for the exhibits.

faqs.q: What can you see in Genoa for free?
faqs.a: The quays of the old port, the outside of Palazzo San Giorgio, the Cathedral of San Lorenzo, the medieval alleys, Via Garibaldi with its palace courtyards, and Porta Soprana.

title: Bruges in a day from Brussels: the belfry climb, the canals, and what is free
subtitle: An hour by train, a loop of four kilometres on foot, and a clear idea of which doors to pay at.
excerpt: How to do Bruges as a day trip from Brussels: the train, a walking loop from the station through the Beguinage to the Markt, how the belfry climb works, what is free, what needs a ticket, and what the partner sells.
longtail_phrases: how to get from Brussels to Bruges by train
how many steps in the Belfry of Bruges
is one day enough for Bruges
what is free to see in Bruges
where is the Michelangelo in Bruges
meta_title: Bruges in a day from Brussels: belfry, canals, free
meta_description: The train from Brussels, a walking loop from the station to the Markt, the 366 steps of the belfry, and what in Bruges is free or needs a ticket.

featured_image.alt: Old brick houses along a canal in Bruges at the Rozenhoedkaai, with the belfry rising behind them

content_html:
[place attraction="belfry-of-bruges" city="bruges"]

Around 1300 Bruges was one of the richest towns in northern Europe. English wool came in, Flemish cloth went out, and merchants from Venice, Genoa and the German ports kept houses here. All of it depended on the Zwin, a tidal inlet that let seagoing ships come within reach of the town. During the fifteenth century the Zwin silted up. The trade moved to Antwerp, and Bruges stopped growing.

For three hundred years almost nothing was built, because nobody had the money to pull the old town down. In 1892 the novel Bruges-la-Morte, by Georges Rodenbach, made its silent canals fashionable, and visitors have come ever since to see a medieval trading town that poverty kept whole. It is small enough for a day from Brussels. The question is how to spend that day, since the best of it is outdoors and free, and the lines form at a few doors.

The train from Brussels

Direct trains run all day from the three main stations of Brussels (Midi, Central and North) and take about an hour. There are no seat reservations: you buy a ticket and take any train. Leave by nine to be in Bruges before the coach groups.

The station is south of the old town. Most people walk straight up the main street to the Markt, which takes twenty minutes. A better way in is to turn right outside the station and enter through the park, which brings you to the quietest corner first.

A loop on foot

  • Minnewater. A long pool that was once a harbour basin for barges, with a park along it. Ten minutes from the station.
  • The Beguinage. A walled court of white houses around a lawn with tall trees, founded in 1245 for beguines, lay women who lived as a religious community. Benedictine nuns have lived here since 1927. The court is free. You are asked to be quiet.
  • The Church of Our Lady. Its brick tower, about 115 metres high, is one of the tallest in the world built of brick. Inside is the Madonna and Child that Michelangelo carved in about 1504 and two merchants of Bruges bought: the only sculpture of his to leave Italy while he was alive.
  • Rozenhoedkaai. The bend of the canal where every photograph of Bruges is taken, with the belfry behind the gables.
  • The Burg. A small square with the Gothic City Hall of 1376 and, in the corner, the Basilica of the Holy Blood: a dark Romanesque chapel below, and above it the chapel that keeps a relic said to have been brought from the Holy Land in the twelfth century.
  • The Markt. The market square, with the belfry on its south side.

Walked without stops, this takes an hour and a half. With stops it fills the day. The way back to the station from the Markt is the twenty-minute main street.

The Beguinage from the water side, with the swans that live on this bank. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The belfry climb

The belfry was the town's strongbox and alarm: its charters were kept here, and its bells ruled the working day. The tower burned in 1280 and was rebuilt. The eight-sided top was added in the 1480s. It once carried a wooden spire, which burned twice and after 1741 was not replaced. The tower is 83 metres high and leans slightly to the east.

There are 366 steps and no lift. The staircase narrows as it climbs, and near the top people going up and coming down share a stone spiral with a rope for a handrail. On the way you pass the old treasury, and the drum of the carillon, which has 47 bells. Only a limited number of visitors are allowed in the tower at one time, so tickets are sold for a time slot and the day's slots can run out by late morning in season. Book ahead, and choose a slot early in your day.

The partner does not sell the belfry. Tickets come from the city's museum service, online or on the spot.

The belfry from below. The eight-sided top stage was added in the 1480s. Photo: Ad Meskens, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The gabled houses of the Markt, from the top of the belfry. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is free, and what is not

  • Free: the Markt and the Burg, the quays, Minnewater, the court of the Beguinage, the chapel of the Holy Blood, St Salvator's Cathedral, and the windmills on the grass rampart at the eastern edge of town.
  • Part free: the Church of Our Lady. You can enter the nave without paying. The part with the Michelangelo and the tombs of Charles the Bold and Mary of Burgundy is a museum with a ticket.
  • Ticket: the belfry, the Gothic Hall of the City Hall, the Groeningemuseum with its paintings by Jan van Eyck and Hans Memling, the treasury of the Holy Blood, and the canal boats.

The boats leave from five landing stages in the centre and make the same half-hour circuit. They are open, so they stop in bad weather, and in the cold months they run less or not at all. You pay at the landing stage.

Michelangelo's Madonna and Child, in its niche in the Church of Our Lady. Photo: Jean-Pol Grandmont, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What the partner sells in Bruges

  • Audio walks through the old town, in the partner's app on your own phone. They follow routes close to the loop above, past the Beguinage, the Church of Our Lady, the Burg and the Markt. They are commentary only: the listings say plainly that entry tickets to the places on the way are not included. Bring earphones.
  • An entry ticket to the Volkskundemuseum, the museum of folk life. It fills a row of seventeenth-century almshouses in the quiet Sint-Anna quarter, a quarter of an hour north-east of the Markt, with a schoolroom, a pharmacy, craftsmen's workshops and a small inn. It suits a second half of the day away from the crowd, and it is close to the windmills.

These are the walks and the ticket our partner sells in Bruges, with today's prices:

[partner city="bruges" match="bruges,brugge,volkskunde" limit="5"]

A room of the Volkskundemuseum: wash tubs, baskets and a wringer. Photo: Rainer Halama, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Timing the day

Between eleven and four the Markt and the Rozenhoedkaai are full of groups. Use those hours for the edges: the Beguinage early, Sint-Anna and the windmills after lunch. Come back to the centre after five, when the day visitors leave and the canals are quiet again. Trains to Brussels run into the evening. Current hours for the tower are on our page for the Belfry of Bruges.

From here

Ghent is on the same railway line, halfway back to Brussels, and makes a second stop if you start early. The coast at Ostend is a quarter of an hour by train in the other direction. See our pages for the Church of Our Lady, the Basilica of the Holy Blood and the rest of Bruges, or open the trip planner for Belgium.

Cover photo: Ank Kumar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How do you get from Brussels to Bruges?
faqs.a: By direct train from Brussels Midi, Central or North, in about an hour. There are no seat reservations. From the station in Bruges the Markt is a twenty-minute walk.

faqs.q: Is one day enough for Bruges?
faqs.a: Yes. The old town is small, and a loop from the station through the Beguinage, the Church of Our Lady, the Burg and the Markt takes an hour and a half without stops. A day leaves time for the belfry and one museum.

faqs.q: How many steps are there in the Belfry of Bruges?
faqs.a: There are 366 steps and no lift. The stairs narrow towards the top. Entry is by time slot because only a limited number of people may be in the tower at once.

faqs.q: What is free to see in Bruges?
faqs.a: The squares, the canalside quays, Minnewater, the court of the Beguinage, the chapel of the Holy Blood, St Salvator's Cathedral, the nave of the Church of Our Lady and the windmills on the eastern rampart.

faqs.q: Where is the Michelangelo in Bruges?
faqs.a: His Madonna and Child is in the Church of Our Lady, in the part of the church that is run as a museum and needs a ticket.

title: Munich's old town on foot: what is free, what needs a ticket, and when the Glockenspiel plays
subtitle: From Marienplatz to the Residenz in two kilometres: three towers, one palace, and a lot that costs nothing.

featured_image.alt: The long neo-Gothic front and the tower of the New Town Hall on Marienplatz in Munich under a blue sky

content_html:
[place attraction="marienplatz" city="munich"]

The Frauenkirche, the cathedral of Munich, was built in twenty years, from 1468 to 1488, which for a church of its size was very fast. Its builder, Jörg von Halsbach, used brick, because there was no stone to be quarried nearby. The money ran out before the towers were finished, and they stood without tops until 1525, when they were given the round green caps they still have, in place of the pointed spires first planned.

Just inside the door there is a dark mark in the floor, shaped like a footprint. The story goes that the devil came to look at the new church, stood on that spot, from which the pillars hid every window, and stamped his foot in delight at a building with no light. The towers are about 99 metres high, and since a vote in 2004 no new building in the city may rise above them. That is why the old town still has the skyline of a place you can walk across in twenty minutes. Most of it costs nothing. A few doors do, and they are worth sorting out before you start.

The route

From Marienplatz, the main square, the walk goes south to St Peter's and the food market, back past the Frauenkirche, then north to the Residenz and Odeonsplatz. It is about two kilometres, flat, and largely closed to cars. Without going inside anything it takes an hour and a half.

The Glockenspiel

The long neo-Gothic building on Marienplatz looks medieval and is not: the New Town Hall was built between 1867 and 1909. In its tower, since 1908, two levels of painted copper figures act out two scenes to the sound of 43 bells. On top, a tournament held in 1568 for the wedding of Duke Wilhelm V, in which the Bavarian knight always wins. Below, the dance of the coopers, said to have brought people back into the streets after a plague.

It plays every day at 11:00 and 12:00, and from March to October also at 17:00. The show lasts about twelve minutes and is free. Stand towards the middle of the square, not under the tower.

The two levels of figures on the tower of the New Town Hall. Photo: Strubbl, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Three towers

  • St Peter's, the oldest parish church of the city, a minute from Marienplatz. Its tower has about 300 steps and no lift, with a narrow balcony all the way round at the top. It is the best of the three views, because it takes in both the Frauenkirche and the town hall. Ticket at the foot of the stairs.
  • The New Town Hall. A lift goes up the 85-metre tower to a viewing gallery. Easier, with a ticket for a time slot, and a view that lacks the building you are standing on.
  • The Frauenkirche. The church is free to enter. Access to its south tower has been closed and reopened over the years: ask at the door.

One tower is enough. If stairs are no trouble, make it St Peter's, and go on a clear day: when the warm south wind blows, the Alps stand along the horizon.

The Frauenkirche from the tower of St Peter's: the view the 300 steps are for. Photo: Diliff, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5.

What is free

  • Marienplatz and the Glockenspiel.
  • The churches. The Frauenkirche, St Peter's, and the Asam Church on Sendlinger Strasse, a tiny Baroque interior that the two Asam brothers built from 1733 beside their own house and filled from floor to ceiling.
  • The Viktualienmarkt. The food market, on this square since 1807, with a maypole and a beer garden under chestnut trees in the middle. Looking is free. The stalls are closed on Sundays.
  • The Hofbräuhaus. The beer hall of the brewery that the dukes of Bavaria founded in 1589. You can walk through the ground floor hall without sitting down.
  • Odeonsplatz. The open hall at its end, the Feldherrnhalle, was built in the 1840s as a copy of the Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence. In front of it, on 9 November 1923, the police stopped Hitler's attempted coup. Beside it stands the yellow Theatine Church, white inside.
  • The Hofgarten, the formal garden behind the Residenz, and the courtyards of the palace, which you can cross.

The stalls of the Viktualienmarkt on a quiet morning. Photo: Wikiolo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What needs a ticket

The towers, as above, and the Residenz. The city palace of the Wittelsbach family, who ruled Bavaria until 1918, grew over four centuries into a block of ten courtyards. It was badly bombed in the Second World War and rebuilt room by room. It is sold in three parts:

  • The Residenz Museum: more than a hundred rooms, among them the Antiquarium, a painted Renaissance hall 66 metres long, begun in 1568 to hold a duke's collection of ancient busts. Allow two hours at least.
  • The Treasury: crowns, jewels and goldwork, in ten rooms. One hour.
  • The Cuvilliés Theatre: a small red and gold court theatre of the 1750s.

Each has its own ticket, and there are combined ones. If you choose a single part, take the museum. Tickets are bought at the palace desk.

The Antiquarium of the Residenz, built from 1568 for a collection of ancient busts. Photo: Jebulon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Audio walks of the old town, several of them, on routes much like the one above: Marienplatz, the Frauenkirche, the Residenz, Odeonsplatz. They are commentary in the partner's app on your own phone, started when you like. The listings state that tickets to the places on the way are not included, so the towers and the palace are paid for separately, on the spot. Bring earphones.
  • An audio walk of legends covers the same streets through their stories, the devil's footprint among them.
  • A Residenz listing that pairs museum entry with an evening concert in the palace. It is a different thing from a plain museum ticket and is tied to a date. Read on the listing which rooms and which hall it covers.

These are the walks and the Residenz evening our partner sells in Munich, with today's prices:

[partner city="munich" match="old town,residenz,legends" limit="6"]

When to go

Be on Marienplatz a little before eleven, watch the Glockenspiel, then climb St Peter's while the crowd is still looking up. Have lunch standing at the market. Keep the Residenz for the afternoon, when you will want to be indoors. On Sundays the shops and the market stalls are shut, and the churches hold services in the morning. Hours for the palace change between summer and winter: see our page for the Munich Residenz.

From here

From the Hofgarten a path leads straight into the English Garden, one of the largest city parks in Europe, with a beer garden at the Chinese Tower. The three Pinakothek galleries are fifteen minutes north-west of Odeonsplatz on foot, and a tram runs west to Nymphenburg Palace. See our pages for Marienplatz, the Frauenkirche and the rest of Munich, or open the trip planner for Germany.

Cover photo: Burkhard Mücke, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: What time does the Glockenspiel play in Munich?
faqs.a: Every day at 11:00 and 12:00, and from March to October also at 17:00. The show on the tower of the New Town Hall lasts about twelve minutes and is free.

faqs.q: Which tower should you climb in Munich?
faqs.a: St Peter's, beside Marienplatz, if you can manage about 300 steps with no lift: its view includes both the Frauenkirche and the town hall. The tower of the New Town Hall has a lift.

faqs.q: What is free to see in the old town of Munich?
faqs.a: Marienplatz and the Glockenspiel, the Frauenkirche, St Peter's and the Asam Church, the Viktualienmarkt, the hall of the Hofbräuhaus, Odeonsplatz, the Hofgarten and the courtyards of the Residenz.

faqs.q: Is the Munich Residenz worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you have two hours. The museum has more than a hundred rooms, including the 66-metre Antiquarium. The Treasury and the Cuvilliés Theatre have their own tickets.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk the old town of Munich?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half from Marienplatz to Odeonsplatz by way of the market, without going inside. With one tower and the Residenz it becomes most of a day.
